The gill edges are gelatinous and easily separating. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 1–3 mm thick, cylindrical, hollow inside, smooth, slippery, yellowish or green-yellowish. Like the cap it is covered with a slippery skin that is easily separated.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena epipterygia occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Poland it is common. A saprotroph developing in coniferous and deciduous forests, on the ground or wood. Fruiting lasts from August to November. It often grows among mosses.
Mycena galericulata (Scop.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–6 cm in diameter, conical-bell-shaped in young specimens, flat with an umbo in older ones, indistinctly wrinkled, bare. Horn-brownish, grey-brown or flesh-brownish in colour, darker in the centre. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are distant, at first whitish, then always slightly pinkish or beige-pink, with a regular trama, sinuately attached to the stem and joined by veins. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick, cylindrical and hollow inside, hard, smooth, shiny, with a rooting base. Colour whitish or greyish. Flesh: Bast-like in the stem, with a faint mealy smell released on rubbing. Taste cucumber-mealy. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores ellipsoid, measuring 9–12 × 6.5–9 μm with a smooth surface, without a germ pore. Basidia two-spored. Similar species: Mycena polygramma – distinguished by a distinctly scalloped stem and in adult specimens the gills are not pinkish; Mycena inclinata is distinguished by a cucumber smell and also lacks pink gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena galericulata is widespread across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Europe it occurs both in the lowlands and in the mountains. In Poland it is very common. It grows in various types of forests. Fungi of this species develop on dead wood of coniferous and deciduous trees, also on forest litter. Fruiting lasts from May to November, and the fruiting bodies often grow in groups.
Mycena haematopus (Pers.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young fruiting bodies, later bell-shaped, conical-bell-shaped with an umbo in older ones. The margin is slightly serrated and usually hung with colourless hyphae (as if with a hem). The surface is smooth, grooved to the middle of the cap, in colour from flesh-brown through reddish-brown to pink-brown. The centre is usually darker. Damaged places discolour blood-red. Gills: Decurrent with a small tooth on the stem or attached to it. Colour in young fruiting bodies from whitish to pink, in older ones darker. Edges smooth. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, up to 3.5 mm thick, cylindrical, hollow inside. The surface is of a similar colour to the cap, entirely covered with small flakes, so that it looks frosted. The base is usually felty. Flesh: Very thin; from a damaged one a blood-red liquid oozes. Taste mild, smell indistinct. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores broadly elliptical, smooth, measuring 8–11 × 5–7 µm, weakly amyloid. Cheilocystidia numerous, spindle-shaped, with elongated and slightly pointed tips. They measure 80 × 12 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and in Europe. In Poland a very common species. It develops on dead wood of deciduous trees: on trunks, stumps and fallen branches. It produces fruiting bodies from April to October. In Poland it has been recorded on the wood of sycamore maple, grey alder, silver birch, cherry, dogwood, hazel, hawthorn, beech, ash, plum, pedunculate oak, sessile oak, black locust, willow and linden. On coniferous trees it occurs rarely.
Mycena pseudocorticola Kühner is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–12 mm in diameter, hemispherical, parabolic, broadly conical to convex, sometimes with a small papilla, often slightly flattened in the centre, grooved, translucent-striate. The surface is dusted, glistening, dark blue, bluish-grey or grey, turning brown with age. Gills: 8–14 reach the stem, fairly broad, convex, broadly attached and decurrent with a short tooth, grey to pale bluish-grey or grey-white, becoming pale sepia-brown with age. Edges lighter. Stem: 5–25 mm tall, 0.2–1 mm thick, straight or bent. The surface is flocculose-dusted, from grey to bluish-grey, more brownish with age. The base is densely covered with long, white fibrils. Flesh: Without smell. Microscopic features: Basidia 25–36 × 9–12 µm, club-shaped, 4-spored with clamp connections, or 2-spored without clamp connections, with swollen sterigmata up to 13 µm long. Spores on 4-spored basidia 8–10.5 × 7.5–10 µm, on 2-spored basidia 13 × 12 µm, spherical or almost spherical, smooth, amyloid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Mycena pseudocorticola is known in some European countries; its occurrence has also been reported in North America and Morocco. Władysław Wojewoda in his 2003 checklist of the large-fruited fungi of Poland cites 10 localities, noting that this species is rare. More recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is classed there as a rare species worth protecting. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland.
Mycena pura (Pers.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The colours of this species are very variable. In young fruiting bodies there are lilac and violet shades, but during maturation they change considerably and the fruiting bodies take on whitish, yellowish, pink, brown and even red colouring. The colour of the fruiting bodies is not sufficient to identify this Mycena. Cap: 2–6 cm in diameter, shape at first convex to bell-shaped, then spread out. The surface is bare, at first lilac-violet, later whitish, yellowish, pink-brown or reddish. Gills: Moderately crowded, sinuately attached to the stem, colour from whitish to grey-white, often flushed pink or violet. Near the stem they are often joined by anastomoses. Stem: 4–10 cm tall, 0.4–0.6 cm thick, cylindrical, hollow, fragile. The surface is shiny, smooth or with fine hairs, whitish or the colour of the cap. Flesh: Watery, whitish or greyish. Smell and taste distinctly resembling radish. Microscopic features: Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores long-elliptical or almost cylindrical, weakly amyloid or non-amyloid, with a smooth surface. They measure 6–10 × 3–4 μm. Basidia with 4 sterigmata.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A widespread species; except Antarctica it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Europe the northern limit of its range runs through Iceland and the northern regions of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Central Europe it is one of the most frequently occurring fungi, and in Poland too it is very common. It produces fruiting bodies from spring to autumn. It occurs in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, in thickets, but also in open areas; in meadows, fallow land, grassy swards and so on.
Mycena renati Quel. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 cm in diameter, bell-shaped in young fruiting bodies, later broadly bell-shaped, finally arched. Margins usually serrated. The surface is smooth. It is hygrophanous. In dry weather it is matt, radially fibrous, and pinkish with a darker apex. In wet weather it becomes grooved with gills showing through, and ranges from yellow-brown to red-brown. It usually has a smaller or larger umbo. Gills: Broad, decurrent with a small tooth, white or slightly pinkish, with smooth edges. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick. It is cylindrical and hollow. The surface is smooth, bare, shiny, golden-yellow or orange-yellow. At the base there is felty mycelium. Flesh: Thin, watery, brittle, yellow in the stem, whitish in the cap. Taste mild, similar to radish; the smell of young fruiting bodies resembles chlorine, of older ones radish. Similar species: Mycena inclinata. It also grows on rotten wood, but has greyish gills and the stem is red-brownish in the lower part; Mycena alcalina. It is distinguished by a smell of ammonia.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs only in Europe. In Poland it occurs mainly in Carpathian beech forest, less often in spruce and pine forests. It usually grows in clumps. It grows in moist forests on dead and already heavily rotten wood of deciduous trees, especially beeches and oaks. It produces fruiting bodies from May to September.
Mycena rosea Gramberg is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, spherical when young, then flat, finally completely spread out. In the centre it has an umbo. It is markedly hygrophanous; when moist the cap is striate because the gills show through. Colour from pale pink to pink, while the umbo in dry weather, as a result of drying, is cream-yellow or yellow. Gills: Distant, bellied, and at the stem notched and narrow. Gill edges smooth. At first white, with time becoming pale pink. Stem: 4–7 cm tall, up to 0.7 cm thick, cylindrical, straight, with a slightly thickened base. Solid in young specimens, tubular in older ones. Colour whitish or white-pink, surface delicately fibrous. Flesh: Thin, white, with a faint taste and smell of radish. Spore print: White. Spores broadly elliptical, amyloid with a smooth surface. On one side they have a bent-back beak. Size: 6–9 × 2.5–4 μm. Similar species: It may be confused with Mycena pura. That Mycena has a more violet shade and occurs in coniferous forests.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Australia and Antarctica. In Europe it is common. A saprotroph. It grows on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests on forest litter, particularly often on calcareous soils. Fruiting bodies appear from May to October.
Mycena tintinnabulum (Paulet) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 0.5–2 cm in diameter, bluntly bell-shaped in young ones, later conical, finally spread out. The centre of the cap is usually flat. The gills show through, as a result of which the cap is radially striate. It is hygrophanous; when moist it is sticky. The surface is bare, smooth, silky shiny, brown, sepia, grey-brown, or dark red-brown, sometimes dark chocolate-brown. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are attached and slightly decurrent with a small tooth, with wavy edges. Intermediate gills are present. At first the gills are light grey with a pinkish tinge, later flesh-pinkish. Stem: 1–7 cm tall, 1–3 mm thick, tubular, bent, hard and cartilaginous. The surface is smooth, slightly sticky when moist, shiny when dry. Pale grey, beige, often reddish at the base and passing into a pseudorhiza covered with protruding white hyphae. Flesh: Very thin, beige-grey, with an indistinct, bitter taste. It has a smell similar to potato peelings or chlorine. The smell quickly fades. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid or stone-shaped with an indistinct beak, with a smooth surface, amyloid and hyaline.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena tintinnabulum occurs mainly in Europe; besides that, in the USA it is known from only a few localities. In Poland it is fairly rare. It grows in various types of forests, parks and avenues on dead wood; on stumps, fallen trunks and boughs of deciduous trees. It has been observed on the wood of grey alder, birches, beeches, oaks and willows. It occurs particularly often on the wood of alders and willows. It produces fruiting bodies from August to December. It is one of the few fungus species that appear very late in autumn and in winter during frost-free periods.
Mycena zephirus (Fr.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, shape at first parabolic or conical, with a rounded umbo, gradually flattening. It is grooved to 2/3 of the diameter. The margin is uneven. The surface is smooth, matt in dry weather, ranging from dirty whitish through light cream and light pink to flesh-brown. The apex of the cap is distinctly darker. On the cap there are rusty-brown, radial spots. Gills: Broad and fairly distant, attached or weakly sinuately notched. They are white-grey, and in older specimens red-brown spots occur on them. Transverse anastomoses are frequent. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, up to 4 mm thick. It is cylindrical, hollow inside (tubular). The surface is fibrillose, grey-brown, covered with short white tufts only at the top. White hairs also occur at the base of the stem. Flesh: Thin, watery and brittle. Grey in colour, taste mild, smell similar to radish. Microscopic features: Basidia with four sterigmata, thickened, measuring 28–32 × 7–8.5 μm. Spores elongated, almost cylindrical, smooth, amyloid, measuring 8.5–12.2 × 4–5 (–6) μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs only in Europe. In Poland it is common. It most often grows in coniferous forests on rotting needles of trees, forest litter, among mosses. It is particularly frequent under spruces and pines. It also occurs in parks. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Mycetinis alliaceus (Jacq.) Earle ex A.W. Wilson & Desjardin is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–4 cm in diameter, shape at first bell-shaped, later convex, finally spread out. Colour fairly variable; from light ochre to dark brown. The surface is matt, dry, sometimes wrinkled, the margin smooth or grooved. Gills: Dirty whitish or greyish, with a regular trama. Stem: Thin and long. It is up to 10 cm tall and 1–2 mm thick. The surface is matt, black-brown or black and white-frosted (felty). The base is rooting. It is tough, fibrous, of cartilaginous consistency and so flexible that it cannot be snapped. Flesh: Thin, whitish. It has a mild taste and a strong smell of garlic. Spore print: White or cream. Spores broadly ellipsoid to almost spherical in shape, smooth, measuring 7–11 × 6–8 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in Europe. In Poland it is not very frequent. It is found in deciduous forests and in parks, always in the presence of beeches. It grows on the ground, on wood debris, especially wood located underground. It produces fruiting bodies from May to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Mycetinis scorodonius. It also has a garlic smell, but is smaller and grows in coniferous forests. Its stem is not black but purple-brown.
Neolentinus lepideus (Fr.) Redhead & Ginns is a species of fungus in the order Gloeophyllales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–11 cm in diameter, conical when young, later flat with a blunt umbo or shallowly depressed in the centre. The surface is matt, dry, cream to light brown, covered with adhering, darker (brown) scales. These scales are larger in the centre, finer near the cap margin. Gills: Broad and broadly attached, running down the stem as far as the ring zone. They have wavy and serrated edges. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, up to 2 cm thick, cylindrical or conical in shape, solid and springy. The surface is whitish; above the ring zone in young specimens there is a felty sheath, below it the stem is covered with scales, and the base itself is brown to black-brown. Flesh: Soft in young specimens, springy, hard and woody in older ones. Whitish, smell sweetish-anise, taste indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 10–15 × 4–5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. A tree-dwelling fungus. It appears in coniferous and mixed forests, but also in cities, on railway sleepers and in coal mines. It develops on roots, beams and posts, mainly on pine and larch wood. It is also not rare on plantations of coniferous trees. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Otidea onotica (Pers.) Fuckel is a species of fungus in the order Pezizales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Ear-shaped on one side, usually with a slit down to the base, bent, somewhat rooting and white-felty; the spore-bearing layer strongly orange to yellow; on the outside delicately mealy. Up to 4 cm wide. Flesh white, without smell, with a mild taste. Similar species: A whole series of species that are hard to tell apart are known. Otidea leporina differs only in its rusty-yellow colour – when young, and later cinnamon-brown. In beech forests the relatively rare Otidea conccinna occurs; it has densely growing, strongly lemon-yellow fruiting bodies, rolled up and slit on one side.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Otidea onotica is recorded in Europe and North America, and besides that its localities have been reported only in Bhutan. In Poland it is relatively rare. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows mostly in small groups in deciduous and coniferous forests.
Mucidula mucida (Schrad.) Pat. is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae. Worldwide there are 15 species of monetka growing in the tropical and temperate zones.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–10 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young specimens, then flatter and flatter, finally spread out with a blunt umbo. The margin is sharp, wrinkled-striate. The surface is pure white or whitish, ivory-coloured, at the top sometimes ochre, sometimes translucent. In wet weather very sticky, slimy and gluey, in dry weather silky matt, smooth. Gills: White, broad, bulging, distant, straight-attached, sinuately notched to slightly decurrent. Stem: 4–10 cm tall, 0.5–1 cm thick, cylindrical, solid, hard, often bent. The surface is smooth, sticky and whitish, brownish only toward the bottom. It has a large drooping or protruding ring. Flesh: White, very thin and soft in the cap, fibrous and hard in the stem. Taste mild, no smell. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: White. Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 14–18 × 12–16 µm. Similar species: It is hard to confuse with other species of fungi, since none of the species growing on wood has such a pure white, porcelain-shiny and slippery cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described only in Europe and East Asia: in Japan, Korea and Taiwan. In Poland it is not very frequent. It grows in forests and parks. Fruiting bodies grow in bundles from June to November, on logs and trunks of dead beeches, often at a great height.
Panellus mitis (Pers.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–2 cm in diameter, shell-shaped, hemispherical or kidney-shaped. Colour whitish, in older specimens turning clay-brown or red-brown. The surface is delicate, felty on young fruiting bodies, smooth on older ones. It is rubbery, sticky and can be peeled off easily. Gills: Crowded and running down the stem. They are white, with coloured, band-like discolourations on the edges. Stem: 2–5 mm long, 3–5 mm thick. It grows laterally, is short, triangular in cross-section and solid. The surface is white, covered with small scales. Sometimes the stem is absent. Flesh: Thin, bast-like, white. Taste mild, no smell. Spore print: White. Spores sausage-shaped, amyloid, measuring 3.5–5 × 1–1.5 μm. Similar species: It may be confused with Crepidotus mollis, which differs among other things in having no stem, or with Pleurocybella porrigens, which also has no stem and is larger.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. In Central Europe it is fairly common. It grows on the wood of coniferous trees; on dead trees, on dead branches hanging or lying on the ground, in brushwood piles. It is a late-autumn and winter fungus, its fruiting bodies appearing mainly from September to April, although sometimes they also appear in summer.
Panellus stipticus (Bull.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–4 cm in diameter, round or kidney-shaped, with a wavy and rolled-under margin. Ochre in colour. The cap skin is matt, at first smooth, in older specimens scaly with a mosaic pattern. Gills: Crowded and clearly delimited from the stem. Colour from pale beige to ochre-brown. Stem: 1–2 cm tall, 0.5 cm thick. It grows laterally, is short and very broad at the point of attachment to the cap. The surface is felty, ochre-brown in colour. Flesh: Thin, bast-like, ochre-coloured. Smell faint, taste bitter, strongly astringent. Spore print: Light ochre. Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, very small, measuring 2–3 × 1–1.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species. Except for Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is very common. It occurs on dead and rotting wood, mainly of deciduous trees, on the wood of coniferous trees very rarely. It grows particularly often on oaks. It usually occurs in clumps.
Panus conchatus (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The vast majority of species in the order Polyporales have a tubular hymenophore. Panus conchatus belongs to a small group of species with a gilled hymenophore. However, phylogenetic studies have shown that despite this distinctness it is closely related to the family Polyporaceae. Cap: 4–12 cm wide, shell-shaped or tongue-shaped, funnel-like depressed in the centre. The surface is smooth or velvety, lilac in young specimens, from ochre to red-brown in older ones. Gills: Running deeply down the stem, crowded, from pale lilac to ochre in colour. Stem: 1–3 cm tall, 1–2 cm thick, eccentric. The surface is felty, colour from ochre-brown to lilac. Flesh: Whitish, bast-like and leathery. Spore print: White. Spores elliptical, non-amyloid, measuring 7–5 × 2.5–3 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Recorded in North, Central and South America, Europe and Asia. It is widespread, but rare everywhere. Its fruiting bodies grow from summer to autumn on dead wood of deciduous trees, mainly on trunks and stumps. It most often occurs in moist riparian forests. It usually occurs gregariously. It grows on various tree species, most often on birches, aspen and oaks. Fruiting bodies grow from July to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Lentinus suavissimus is similar, but differs in its anise smell, is smaller and grows only on willows.
Parasola auricoma (Pat.) Redhead, Vilgalys & Hopple is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: At maturity it reaches 1–6 cm in diameter. At first egg-shaped, then slightly conical or convex, finally almost flat. Over almost the whole surface it is deeply, radially grooved. The surface seen with the naked eye is smooth, under a hand lens finely hairy, orange-brown in young fruiting bodies, greyish in older ones. No veil remnants. Gills: Free or almost free, moderately crowded, at first whitish, then dark grey, finally black. Stem: 3–12 cm tall, up to 3 mm in diameter, cylindrical, brittle, hollow inside. The surface is smooth or delicately silky, in colour from whitish to slightly yellowish. No ring. Flesh: Thin, without smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spore print black. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 10–16 × 6–9 µm; with a central germ pore, dark brown in KOH. Basidia 4-sterigmate. Cheilocystidia cylindrical, spindle-shaped or sac-shaped, about 90 × 25 µm. Pleurocystidia similar; up to about 130 × 35 µm. In the hymenium there are scattered or abundant thick-walled setae, up to about 400 × 10 µm, dark red in KOH. Clamp connections present. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Parasola auricoma is known in Europe, both Americas, Asia and New Zealand. It is common, but is often confused with other species, especially Parasola plicatilis. W. Wojewoda in 2003 gives 7 localities in Poland. B. Gierczyk in 2011 gives 5 more. Numerous and more recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is classed there as a threatened species worth protecting. A saprotroph. Found on the ground and on wood chips in meadows, lawns and roadsides.
